health-psychology-s3.title: Daily hassles and colds
health-psychology-s3.html:
Introduction

Researchers asked whether people who report more daily hassles also report more days of cold symptoms.

Participants

150 adults (ages 25 to 60) living in one city in Canada, recruited through online ads. All gave informed consent and were told they could leave the study at any time. Names were replaced by code numbers.

Method

Each evening for eight weeks, participants rated how many hassles they had that day on a 0 to 10 scale and noted whether they had cold symptoms. The researchers compared each person's average hassle score with their total days of symptoms.

Results

People with higher average hassle scores tended to have more days of cold symptoms (r=0.35r = 0.35).

Invented study for practice.

positive-psychology-s3.title: Who bounces back after a hurricane?
positive-psychology-s3.html:
Introduction

Researchers asked how common resilience is after a major disaster, and which factors go with it.

Participants

480 adults living in coastal towns in Louisiana that were damaged by a hurricane. All gave informed consent. Data were stored without names.

Method

Participants completed a distress questionnaire (scored 0 to 40) at 3, 12 and 24 months after the hurricane, and reported how many people they could count on for help. Each person was classified as resilient (low distress at all three times), recovering (high, then falling), or chronic (high at all three times).

Results

Resilient: 62% of participants. Recovering: 23%. Chronic: 15%. People who reported more sources of support were more likely to be resilient.

Invented study for practice.

explaining-disorders-s3.title: Does a diagnostic label change how people judge a coworker?
explaining-disorders-s3.html:
Introduction

Researchers asked whether knowing that someone has a diagnosed psychological disorder changes how willing people are to work with that person.

Participants

120 college students from one university volunteered. Each read a consent form and agreed in writing to take part, and the university's institutional review board approved the study.

Method

Each student read the same one-page description of a coworker, "Sam," who is quiet, works carefully and sometimes misses lunch with the team. Students were randomly assigned to one of two versions. In the label version, one added sentence said that Sam has a diagnosed psychological disorder; in the no-label version, that sentence was left out. Each student then rated "How willing would you be to work on a project with Sam?" from 1 (not at all) to 7 (very willing). Afterward, students were told the purpose of the study.

Results

The mean willingness rating was 4.1 in the label version and 5.6 in the no-label version. The difference was statistically significant.

Discussion

The same description led to lower willingness when a label was added, which suggests that diagnostic labels can carry stigma.

Invented study for practice.

disorders-s3.title: Hurricane exposure and later PTSD symptoms
disorders-s3.html:
Introduction

Researchers asked whether adults who went through more of a hurricane's dangers would report more symptoms of posttraumatic stress six months later.

Participants

Seven adults, ages 24 to 61, from one coastal town volunteered after reading flyers at a community center. Each gave informed consent, and the researchers kept every name confidential by giving each person a number.

Method

Each adult reported how many of eight hurricane dangers they had faced (for example, flooding in the home or being injured). Six months later, each completed a 20-item symptom checklist about flashbacks, avoidance, mood and feeling on edge; the total score could range from 0 to 80. The researchers did not assign anyone to a level of danger.

Results

Symptom scores were 8, 12, 15, 22, 30, 41 and 48. Adults who had faced more dangers tended to have higher scores (correlation r=0.78r = 0.78).

Discussion

Greater exposure to the hurricane's dangers went with more symptoms of posttraumatic stress.

Invented study for practice.

treatment-s1.title: Therapy, medication or a waitlist for depression
treatment-s1.html:
Introduction

Researchers asked whether cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) and antidepressant medication each reduce symptoms of depression more than waiting for treatment.

Participants

150 adults ages 18 to 65, all diagnosed with major depressive disorder by a clinician, were recruited from three community clinics in one US state. Each gave written informed consent after being told the risks of each treatment and that they could leave the study at any time. A university institutional review board approved the study.

Method

Participants were randomly assigned to 12 weeks of weekly CBT sessions, 12 weeks of an SSRI antidepressant, or a 12-week waitlist (they were offered treatment when the study ended). Depression was measured with a 21-item symptom questionnaire (scores from 0 to 63; higher scores mean more severe symptoms), given before and after the 12 weeks by an interviewer who did not know each person's group.

Results

Mean scores fell from 30 to 16 in the CBT group, from 30 to 17 in the medication group, and from 30 to 26 in the waitlist group. The CBT and medication groups each improved significantly more than the waitlist group; the difference between CBT and medication was not statistically significant.

Discussion

Both treatments outperformed waiting, and neither clearly outperformed the other over 12 weeks.

Invented study for practice.

items.q: Ines is nervous but excited about starting her dream job. The challenge pushes her to learn quickly and she feels energized. Which concept describes this kind of stress?
Over a month, Cole deals with a slow laptop, long lines at the cafeteria, a noisy roommate and lost keys. Researchers would classify these as which kind of stressor?
A deer freezes in the headlights of a car, and a hiker who meets a bear stands perfectly still. Which response do these examples show?
After a tornado damages their town, many parents gather their children close and then join neighbors to share food and look after one another. Which stress response does this best illustrate?
Lena is stressed about a chemistry test next week. She makes a study schedule, forms a study group and asks the teacher for practice problems. Which coping strategy is she using?
Marco's grandmother has died. He cannot change what happened, so he talks with friends, journals about his feelings and goes for long walks. Which coping strategy fits best?
A student facing a stressor she can partly control decides which coping strategy to use. Which choice best matches the research on coping?
options: Use emotion-focused coping, since changing problems rarely works
Avoid coping until the stressor passes on its own
Use problem-focused coping, even on parts she has no control over
Act on the parts she can change and manage feelings about the rest

items.q: In a study of thousands of adults, those who reported four or more adverse childhood experiences had higher rates of heart disease decades later. Which conclusion is justified?
options: Adverse childhood experiences directly cause heart disease in most adults who have them
They are linked to poorer later health, but other variables may contribute
Heart disease in adulthood causes people to recall more childhood stress
There is no link between childhood stress and adult health

items.q: Which field studies how psychological factors such as stress, behavior and social support affect physical health and illness?
Which stage of the general adaptation syndrome do weeks 3 to 7 best represent?

options: The alarm reaction makes people sick at the start of stress
Eustress protects people from illness, so the students got sick from boredom
Resistance is highest at the end of a long stressor

items.q: In the figure, why does resistance first dip below normal?

The sudden stressor causes shock before sympathetic arousal begins
The stressor has ended and the body is recovering

items.q: A worker has had a high-pressure job for two years with no breaks. He now catches every cold that goes around. Which stage of the figure does he most likely match?
The general adaptation syndrome was first described from studies of rats exposed to many kinds of stressors. Which statement is most accurate about applying it to people?
options: It does not apply to people, because it came from studies of rats
The broad pattern fits people, but appraisal and coping change it
It shows that stress of any kind is harmful to physical health
It shows that people go through each stage at the same speed

items.q: Two students face the same hard final exam. One sees it as a threat she cannot handle; the other sees it as a challenge she can prepare for. The second student shows less distress. What best explains the difference?
options: How each student appraised the stressor
The exam was a daily hassle for one and not the other
One student was in the alarm stage and the other in exhaustion
One of them lacks a working sympathetic nervous system

items.q: A research team studies what helps ordinary people thrive: what makes work meaningful, which habits raise life satisfaction, and how communities support flourishing. Which field best describes their work?
In a survey, Ana rates her life satisfaction 9 out of 10 and reports feeling many more pleasant than unpleasant emotions. Which concept do these ratings measure?
After her family lost their home in a fire, Kiara felt shaken for weeks, then gradually returned to school, sports and friendships, functioning much as before. Which concept best describes her?

A year after a serious car accident, Dev says he now values his relationships more, feels stronger than he thought he was, and changed his career to something more meaningful. Which concept do these changes show?
Every night for two weeks, students write down three things that went well that day and why. Which positive psychology concept is this exercise designed to build?

A teacher notices that Mateo is at his best when he is curious and learning new things, and he says those moments feel most like "the real me." In positive psychology, what are these strengths called?

items.q: A school asks students to use one of their top strengths in a new way each day for a week. Several studies of similar exercises found small gains in happiness. Which conclusion is most accurate?
options: Using strengths guarantees lasting happiness for the students
The exercise may raise well-being a little, though effects are small
Strengths exercises help students with low well-being but harm the rest
The gains prove that strengths are inherited

items.q: Sofia speaks up for a classmate who is being teased, even though it might make her unpopular. Under which virtue category in the figure does her strength belong?
A team captain makes sure every player gets equal playing time and organizes the team well. Which virtue category in the figure do these strengths fall under?
A grandfather forgives a relative who hurt him years ago and keeps his temper in check. Which virtue category best fits?
By how many points did the gratitude group's mean life satisfaction rise from before to after?

0.1 is the neutral group's change. Use the gratitude row.

items.q: What does "statistically significant, but the effect size was small" mean for these results?
options: The difference was large and mattered for each of the students
The difference was probably due to chance
It is unlikely to be chance, but it is modest in size
The study was not an experiment, so no conclusion is possible

items.q: Why did the researchers include a neutral-writing group instead of only measuring the gratitude group before and after?
options: To turn the study into a correlational study of writing and mood
To rule out time passing or writing itself as the cause

To protect the confidentiality of the students' journals

items.q: Which conclusion do the results best support?
options: Resilience was the most common outcome after the disaster
Most people developed long-lasting distress after the disaster
Resilience is rare and found mainly in exceptional people

items.q: Which research design did the researchers use to classify each person's pattern over time?
What percent of participants were not in the resilient group?

items.q: A reader wants to apply these findings to teenagers after a wildfire in another country. What is the main limit on doing so?
options: The sample of 480 is too small to say anything about teenagers
The distress questionnaire used a range of scores from 0 to 40
The researchers stored the data under codes instead of names
Participants were Louisiana adults after a hurricane, not teens

items.q: Write the operational definition of resilience used in this study.

specific.frame: A person was classified as resilient if they had ___ at ___.
specific.model: A person was classified as resilient if they had low scores on the 0 to 40 distress questionnaire at all three times: 3, 12 and 24 months after the hurricane.

opdef.label: Operational definition
options: low scores on the 0 to 40 distress questionnaire
a strong, positive attitude toward life
many people they could count on for help

why.1: An attitude is a general description, not the measure the study used.
why.2: Support was a separate variable measured alongside resilience.

why.1: Resilience required low distress at every one of the three times.

items.q: A news story claims that "positive thinking cures illness" and that people who stay upbeat will beat any disease. How should a psychology student evaluate this claim?
options: Accept it, because positive psychology has proven it
Accept it, because subjective well-being is a medical treatment
Doubt it: optimism has modest links to health, but links are not cures
Reject positive psychology as a field, because it studies happiness

items.q: Dana has felt low most of the day for five weeks. She has stopped going to her classes and lost her part-time job because she cannot get out of bed on time. Which part of the definition of a psychological disorder do the missed classes and the lost job show most directly?
options: Deviation: the pattern is unusual for her culture
Distress: the pattern causes her inner suffering
Diathesis: the pattern comes from a vulnerability
Dysfunction: it interferes with daily life

items.q: Theo lives alone in a cabin without electricity, dyes his hair bright green and plays the accordion at midnight. He is content, keeps steady work as a carpenter and has close friends. Why would a clinician most likely not diagnose a psychological disorder?
options: His behavior is too common to count as deviation
He lives alone, so no one can observe his symptoms
His unusual behavior causes no distress or dysfunction
He has no diathesis, so a disorder is impossible for him

items.q: In one community, people in mourning are expected to speak aloud to a relative who has died, at a family altar, for several weeks. A visiting clinician from another country first thinks this behavior is a sign of a disorder. Which idea best explains the clinician's error?
options: Distress is the single criterion that decides a diagnosis
Deviation depends on the person's own cultural norms
The diathesis-stress model says that grief causes disorders
The behavior is a symptom, so the culture does not matter

items.q: A clinic in Brazil records each diagnosis with a code from the classification system published by the World Health Organization, which health systems in many countries use for all illnesses. Which system is the clinic using?
options: The biopsychosocial model of psychological disorders
The eclectic approach to classifying and treating

items.q: After a large dog bit him at age seven, Luis began to panic whenever he saw any dog, and he crossed the street to avoid them. A psychologist says his fear was learned by pairing dogs with pain and is kept going because avoiding dogs brings relief. Which perspective is the psychologist using?

Priya gets one low quiz grade and thinks, "This proves I am stupid and will fail at everything." She feels hopeless for days. A psychologist says her low mood comes mostly from the way she interprets events. Which perspective explains her mood this way?

A therapist suggests that a client's constant worry may come from conflicts he is unaware of, rooted in his relationship with a demanding parent, which he keeps out of awareness with defense mechanisms. Which perspective is the therapist using?

Fears of snakes, heights and the dark are far more common than fears of cars or electrical outlets, even though cars and outlets injure more people today. Which perspective best explains this pattern?

Growing up, Jonah felt loved only when he earned top grades. Now he feels empty and anxious because the person he believes he must be does not match how he actually feels and acts. Which perspective explains his distress this way?

A clinician assessing Rosa notes three things: her mother and grandmother both had long periods of depression; Rosa tends to blame herself for anything that goes wrong; and she recently lost her job in a town with few others. Which approach is the clinician using?

A therapist helps one client change self-critical thoughts, teaches another to face feared situations step by step, and with a third explores how childhood relationships still shape her choices. She picks methods from different perspectives to fit each person. What is this called?

Identical twins Ana and Bea share the same genes. Both have a family history that raises their risk of depression. Ana loses her home in a flood and goes through a long period of depression; Bea, living elsewhere, faces no major losses and does not. Which model best explains the difference?

A psychologist studying depression in different countries finds that it is diagnosed more often in groups facing poverty, discrimination and job loss. She concludes that social conditions shape who develops depression. Which perspective is she using?
In the figure, why does Person 2 stay below the threshold while Person 1 passes it, even though both face the same small stress?
options: Person 2 faces a larger stress than Person 1 does
Person 1 has no vulnerability, just stress
Person 1 starts with a much larger vulnerability
Person 2 is above the threshold as well

items.q: According to the model in the figure, what would most likely happen if Person 2 later faced a stress as large as Person 3's?
options: Person 2 would stay below the threshold
Person 2 would also pass the threshold
The threshold for Person 2 would rise

items.q: Which real situation fits the pattern shown for Person 3?
options: Someone with no family history becomes depressed after several severe losses
A person with a strong family history develops depression after a minor argument
A person with a strong family history stays well through a calm, easy year
A person with no family history stays well after a minor argument with a friend

items.q: Which group in the table had the highest percent with a period of depression?
options: Adults without a family history and 3 or more events
Adults with a family history and 0 events
Adults with a family history and 1 or 2 events
Adults with a family history and 3 or more events

items.q: Among adults with a family history, how many percentage points higher was the rate of depression with 3 or more stressful events than with 0 events?

mistakes.why: 32% is the rate with 3 or more events. Subtract the rate with 0 events, 10%, to get the difference.
That difference, 14 minus 6, is for adults without a family history. Use the "Yes" row.

items.q: How do the data in the table best support the diathesis-stress model?
options: Adults with no family history had no periods of depression
Stressful events raised the rate far more for adults with a family history
Stressful events made no difference to the rate
Family history made the same difference at each level of stress

items.q: The researchers measured family history and stressful events as they occurred and did not assign them. What can they conclude?
options: Stress and family history are linked to depression, but not that they cause it
Stressful events cause depression in people with a family history
Family history has no relationship with depression
The results apply to adults in other countries as well

items.q: Which research method did this study use?
Write the operational definition of willingness to work with Sam, as this study measured it.

specific.frame: Willingness was measured as ___ on a ___ scale.
specific.model: Willingness was measured as each student's rating of "How willing would you be to work on a project with Sam?" on a 1 (not at all) to 7 (very willing) scale.

opdef.label: Operational definition
options: each student's rating of "How willing would you be to work on a project with Sam?"
how much each student liked Sam as a person
whether Sam had a diagnosed disorder

why.1: Liking Sam was not measured. The study asked about working on a project.
why.2: That is the independent variable, what was manipulated, not what was measured.

why.1: The rating was not a yes or no answer. Students chose a number from 1 to 7.
why.2: The scale ran from 1 to 7, not 0 to 100.

items.q: What does it mean that the difference between 4.1 and 5.6 was statistically significant?
options: Each student in the label version gave a rating of 4.1
A difference this large is unlikely to be due to chance alone
The label made the difference in willingness very large
The results will apply to workers in other countries

items.q: Which ethical safeguard does the summary say the researchers used?
options: Written informed consent from each student before taking part
Random assignment of students to the two versions
Payment to each student who completed the rating
A follow-up interview a year after the study

items.q: For the past three years, Marcus has felt low on most days, with poor appetite and low energy. He keeps working and seeing friends, but he says he cannot remember the last time he felt good for more than a week or two. Which disorder best fits this pattern?

For ten days, Jordan has slept two or three hours a night yet feels full of energy. He talks so fast that friends cannot follow, has spent his savings on a plan to start five companies, and says he is destined to be famous. He has never had a depressive episode. Which disorder best fits?

Last year, Kim had a major depressive episode that lasted two months. This spring she had five days of unusually high energy: she slept less, felt very confident and started many projects, though she kept going to work and nobody needed to step in. Which diagnosis fits this history best?
A man with schizophrenia hears a voice commenting on everything he does, even when he is alone in a quiet room. What is this symptom?

Elena firmly believes that her neighbors have put a device in her wall to read her thoughts. When her brother shows her the empty wall, she says the device must be invisible. Which symptom does this show?

A news story calls a woman with schizophrenia a person with a "split personality." Why is that description wrong?
options: Schizophrenia is a mood disorder, not a psychotic one
Schizophrenia involves a break from reality, not separate identities
Schizophrenia involves several identities, not one split
Schizophrenia begins in early childhood, not later

items.q: Friends notice that Ruth sometimes speaks and acts like a very different person, with a different name, voice and handwriting, and afterward she has no memory of what happened during those times. Which disorder do these symptoms describe?

A man is found working at a diner in a city 400 miles from home. He cannot recall his name, his family or how he got there. Doctors find no head injury or drug use, and his memory loss began right after a frightening event. Which diagnosis fits best?

Several times over the past few months, Sasha has suddenly felt her heart pound, her chest tighten and an overwhelming fear that she was dying, once while sitting calmly on her couch. Since then she worries every day about the next attack. Which disorder best fits?

Omar stopped riding the bus, going to the mall and standing in lines, because he fears he would not be able to get out or get help if he started to panic. He now rarely leaves his apartment. Which disorder fits best?

Leah is a strong student but has skipped every class presentation this year. Days before each one, she imagines classmates laughing at her shaking voice, and she feels sick with fear of being judged. Which disorder best fits?

For more than a year, Paolo has worried most days about his grades, his parents' health, money and the news. He cannot turn the worry off, sleeps poorly, feels tense and tires easily. Nothing specific sets it off. Which disorder fits best?

Nadia has unwanted thoughts that she left the stove on and will cause a fire. She knows the thought is unlikely, but it makes her so anxious that she checks the stove 20 times before leaving home, which makes her late every day. Which disorder best fits?

Glen's house is so full of old newspapers, broken appliances and empty boxes that he cannot use his kitchen or sit on his couch. When his sister offers to clear some out, he becomes very upset and insists he may need every item. Which disorder fits best?

Three months after a serious car crash, Ana has nightmares and vivid flashbacks of the crash, avoids driving and the road where it happened, feels on edge and jumps at sudden noises. Which disorder best fits?

A 17-year-old has a weight in the normal range. Several times a week she eats a very large amount of food in a short time while feeling out of control, then tries to make up for it by fasting or exercising for hours. Which disorder best fits?

Since first grade, Theo has had trouble finishing tasks, loses his homework, is easily distracted and often interrupts. His parents see the same pattern at home, and his teachers see it at school. Which disorder fits best?

A four-year-old rarely makes eye contact, does not point to share interest, and has trouble with back-and-forth play. He lines up his toy cars in the same order each day and becomes very upset if anyone moves one. Which disorder do these signs suggest a clinician would assess for?

For as long as anyone can remember, Victor has believed that coworkers, neighbors and even relatives are secretly plotting against him. He reads hidden insults into kind remarks and trusts no one. To which cluster of personality disorders does this pattern belong?
options: No cluster: this is a delusion

items.q: Since his early teens, a 30-year-old man has repeatedly lied to and cheated people, broken laws, and shown no remorse for harming others. To which personality disorder does this lasting pattern point?

Mei insists that every report at work follow her exact rules. She rechecks details so often that projects miss their deadlines and she refuses to let others help. She has no unwanted, intrusive thoughts; she sees her standards as simply correct. Which diagnosis fits best?

In Japan, a young man feels intense fear that his body odor and gaze make other people uncomfortable, so he avoids eye contact and meetings. Which concept from the course does this example illustrate?

Some stimulant drugs that increase dopamine activity can, at high doses, produce hallucinations and delusions in people with no history of a disorder, while drugs that block dopamine receptors tend to reduce these symptoms. Which explanation do these findings support?

items.q: A doctor lists symptoms seen in people with schizophrenia. Which of them are positive symptoms? Select all that apply.

Showing almost no emotion in the face or voice
Believing that a TV host is sending secret messages

items.q: A student sees that "Depressive" and "Bipolar" are separate boxes in the figure. What best explains why they are separated?

Bipolar disorders are a kind of personality disorder

What pattern does the graph show?

options: Children who have lived through any kind of disaster

options: Debriefing: adults were told after the study that they had been deceived
Random assignment: adults were placed in danger groups by chance

items.q: Which person's ratings show a period of very high mood followed later by a period of very low mood?

3 is the median, the middle of the ordered ratings. The mean divides the sum by 4.

items.q: Person A's low period lasts four weeks. Which DSM-5-TR rule makes that long enough to count as a major depressive episode, if the other symptoms are present?
options: At least two years of symptoms
At least six months of symptoms
At least two weeks of symptoms
At least one day of symptoms

items.q: Lying on a couch, a client is asked to say whatever comes to mind, however silly or embarrassing, while the therapist listens for patterns that may reveal hidden conflicts. Which technique is this?

A therapist mostly listens. She restates what her client says ("It sounds like you felt invisible at that dinner"), never judges him, and lets him lead each session, trusting that he can find his own way forward. Which therapy is she using?

Ines is terrified of elevators. Her therapist first teaches her deep muscle relaxation. Then, while relaxed, she imagines a list of scenes from least to most frightening, starting with looking at a photo of an elevator and ending with riding one to the top floor. Which technique is this?

A person who wants to stop drinking alcohol takes a medication that makes him feel sick whenever he drinks. Over time, the taste of alcohol alone makes him feel queasy. Which technique is this, and what learning does it rely on?
options: Exposure therapy, using extinction of fear
Biofeedback, using signals from the body

items.q: On a hospital unit, patients earn plastic chips for making their beds, attending group sessions and taking their medication. They trade the chips for snacks, phone time or outings. Which technique is this?
Watching a screen that shows her muscle tension as a rising line, a woman with frequent tension headaches learns to relax her forehead and jaw until the line drops. Which technique is this?

A therapist tells a client who keeps saying "I must be liked by everyone or I am worthless": "Where is the evidence that you must be liked by everyone? Is it a disaster, or just disappointing, if one person does not like you?" Which therapy is this?

A therapist notices that her client with depression sees himself as a failure, expects the future to be hopeless, and believes everyone thinks badly of him. Which concept describes this set of thoughts?

A teen who has strong emotional swings and has harmed herself joins a program that teaches mindfulness, ways to tolerate distress and skills for handling relationships, balanced with acceptance of who she is. Which therapy is this?

A family therapist meets with a teenager, his parents and his sister together, because she sees the teen's problems as part of how the whole family communicates. What is the main advantage of this format over individual sessions?
options: It is the best-supported format for each disorder
It removes the need for a therapeutic alliance with the teen
It works on patterns in the relationships that the problem is part of
It lets the therapist prescribe medication to the family

items.q: Two therapists use the same method. Clients of the first, whom they describe as warm, trusting and working with them on shared goals, improve more than clients of the second. Which concept best explains the difference?

A therapist working with a family who recently moved from Somalia asks them how they understand the son's distress, what healing means in their community, and admits what she does not yet know about their culture. Which concept does this show?

Starting in the 1950s, US state hospitals released many long-term patients to live in their communities, helped by new antipsychotic drugs. Too few community services followed. Which term describes this shift, and what was one result?
options: Psychosurgery; many people lost their memory
Cultural humility; therapists learned new cultures
The therapeutic alliance; patients trusted doctors

items.q: A woman with bipolar I disorder takes a medication that evens out her mood and makes manic episodes less likely, and she has regular blood tests because the right dose is close to a harmful dose. Which medication is this?

A man with schizophrenia has fewer hallucinations after he starts a medication that blocks dopamine receptors. After years on an older drug of this kind, he develops repeated, involuntary movements of his lips and tongue. What is the drug, and what is the side effect?

A man with severe depression has not improved with two medications and several months of therapy. With his informed consent, under anesthesia and with a muscle relaxant, doctors pass a brief electric current through his brain to cause a short seizure, several times over a few weeks. Which treatment is this?

While a woman with depression sits awake in a chair, a coil held against her scalp sends repeated magnetic pulses to an area of her prefrontal cortex, five days a week for several weeks. Which treatment is this?
A woman asks a hypnotist to help her "recover" memories from early childhood. Based on research, what is the most accurate response?
options: Hypnosis reliably brings back accurate early memories
Hypnosis lets people relive childhood exactly as it happened
Hypnosis can increase confidence in memories without making them more accurate
Hypnosis has no use in treatment of any kind

items.q: A psychologist chooses a treatment for a client by combining the best available research on that problem, her own clinical skill, and the client's values, culture and preferences. What is this approach called?
A client tells her therapist that she is struggling at work. Later, her boss calls the therapist to ask how the client is doing. What should the therapist do, and why?
options: Not share anything, because of confidentiality
Share a short summary, because the boss is concerned
Share everything, because the job is at stake
Tell the boss the diagnosis but nothing else

items.q: A man with panic disorder is prescribed a fast-acting drug that increases the calming effect of GABA. His doctor warns him to use it only for a short time. Why the warning?
options: The drug works after several weeks of daily use
The drug blocks dopamine and causes tardive dyskinesia
The drug is a mood stabilizer that needs blood tests
These drugs can lead to tolerance and dependence

items.q: Put the steps of exposure-based treatment for a fear of dogs in the order a therapist would use them, from first to last.
options: Build a list of dog situations ranked from least to most frightening
Look at photos of dogs until the fear drops
Stand across the room from a calm, leashed dog
Pet a calm dog while the therapist is nearby

items.q: What was the independent variable in this study?

The treatment condition each person received
The participants' ages, from 18 to 65 years
Whether the interviewer knew each person's group

To give the waitlist group a different medication
To make sure the groups had identical starting scores
To test whether waiting causes depression to get worse

options: CBT and medication had no effect on symptoms
Medication was better than CBT for most participants
The study was not ethical, so its results do not count

items.q: Which conclusion do the data in the graph best support?
options: Medication lowered anxiety more than exposure therapy or waiting
The waitlist group improved as much as the medication group
Exposure lowered anxiety most; both treatments beat waiting
No group changed from before to after treatment

items.q: The waitlist group's mean fell by 3 points with no treatment. Which idea best explains why researchers expect some change in a control group like this?
options: The waitlist group secretly received exposure therapy
Symptoms can ease with time, and expecting help can matter
Anxiety scores fall from one test to the next by rule
The waitlist group had a different disorder from the others

items.q: Suppose the 60 adults had been randomly assigned to the three groups. Why would that let researchers say exposure therapy caused the larger drop?
options: The groups would be alike on average before treatment
The adults would be a random sample of all people with anxiety
The anxiety scores would be measured without error
The researchers would know the true population mean score
